pages.title: Chacoan culture: a regional ancestral Pueblo world
pages.intro: Chacoan culture describes a regional pattern of architecture, connections, and practices, with Chaco Canyon as an important centre. It should not be equated automatically with a single ethnic group, language, or uniform political state.

paragraphs.text: Great kivas, formal open spaces, sacred landscapes, and orientations toward celestial cycles support Chaco's ceremonial importance. Pueblo descendants describe it as a gathering place for peoples and clans with different traditions. Some researchers interpret roads as ritual or symbolic connections; others also emphasize practical transport. These interpretations do not establish one uniform religion or reveal every ceremony performed in the canyon.

No single spoken language is established for all Chacoan communities. Keres has been proposed as an important language at Chaco, but that remains a scholarly interpretation. Shared ceremonial imagery or architectural forms cannot independently identify speech. NPS cautions that rock imagery is not a translatable language record, while descendant communities maintain distinct interpretations and connections. Cultural affiliation should not be converted into a one-language census.

Monumental building began in the mid-800s, and by about 1050 Chaco had broad ceremonial, administrative, and economic importance. During the 1100s and 1200s construction slowed and regional roles shifted toward other centres. Drought was a substantial challenge, but a single climatic cause does not explain every change. Migration and reorganization continued living histories whose descendants include multiple Pueblo communities and Navajo clans.

pages.title: Chaco Canyon: great houses, community spaces, and engineered roads
pages.intro: Chaco's monumental buildings belong to a regional history of ceremony, exchange, and coordinated construction. Their scale is visible; the precise organization of authority and the functions of particular spaces require interpretation.

sections.heading: Reading the canyon as a connected place

paragraphs.text: NPS places Chaco's prominence between about 850 and 1250 CE. Its multistory public and ceremonial buildings required deliberate design, engineering, and the organization of substantial labor. Architectural sophistication demonstrates coordinated work, but does not by itself identify a particular political system.

A great house is a monumental architectural category, not a population count. Rooms could serve multiple purposes; the number of rooms should not be presented as the number of residents. Compare the excavated spaces of Pueblo Bonito with the largely buried remains of Hungo Pavi before treating their present appearances as an original difference in size or importance.

sections.heading: Principal great houses and the great kiva

rows.name: Pueblo Bonito
rows.dates: Constructed in stages, about 850–1150 CE.
rows.architecture: A D-shaped complex that at its height had more than 600 rooms, about 40 kivas, two plazas, and four to five stories in places.
rows.limits: Architectural totals summarize a building that changed through time. They are not a simultaneous resident census, and 'palace' or royal residence is not established by its size.

rows.name: Una Vida
rows.dates: Initial building around 850 CE.
rows.architecture: An early multistory great house with distinctive masonry and a great kiva, near the present visitor center.
rows.limits: Only minor excavation and preservation work has occurred. Much of its form remains buried, so the standing walls understate the original complex.

rows.name: Hungo Pavi
rows.dates: Chacoan great-house period; a precise building sequence is not supplied by the cited visitor page.
rows.architecture: More than 150 rooms, a great kiva, and an enclosed plaza; a stairway survives on the cliff behind it.
rows.limits: Unexcavated remains are largely protected by sand and vegetation. Do not interpret their low profile as a small original structure.

rows.name: Chetro Ketl
rows.dates: Multiple building episodes; exact construction dates are not specified in the cited site page.
rows.architecture: The second-largest Chacoan great house covers more than three acres. Great and elevated kivas accompany an elevated plaza about 12 feet above the canyon floor.
rows.limits: Second- and third-story construction and plaza raising created the visible form over time; do not assume a single building event.

rows.name: Pueblo del Arroyo
rows.dates: About 1065–1150 CE, in two comparatively short phases.
rows.architecture: A great house built in the open near the arroyo rather than against the canyon cliffs; its unusual tri-wall structure is the only example NPS identifies in Chaco Canyon.
rows.limits: The tri-wall form is distinctive, but its presence alone does not demonstrate a specific ethnic identity or political relationship.

rows.name: Casa Rinconada
rows.dates: Part of the Chacoan community landscape; precise dates are not supplied by the cited overview.
rows.architecture: A very large excavated great kiva on the south side of the canyon, among smaller house sites.
rows.limits: Potential astronomical alignments have been proposed. The surrounding buildings also record remodeling and construction over older structures.

rows.name: Wijiji
rows.dates: Early 1100s CE; uniform construction suggests a concentrated building episode around 1110–1115.
rows.architecture: A strongly symmetrical great house with uniform masonry and rooms. Its layout lacks an enclosed plaza and an incorporated great kiva.
rows.limits: Its apparently brief construction contrasts with repeatedly enlarged great houses. Suggestions that it was unfinished remain interpretations.

rows.name: Pueblo Alto and New Alto
rows.dates: Chacoan great-house landscape; exact dates are not established by the cited trail page.
rows.architecture: Mesa-top great houses reached by the Pueblo Alto Trail, in a landscape of roads, ramps, stairways, and broad views across the basin.
rows.limits: Use these sites to study connections between canyon floor and mesa, without treating visibility as proof of centralized control.

sections.heading: What the roads show—and what remains debated

paragraphs.text: Chacoan roads often follow conspicuously straight alignments. NPS describes canyon roads averaging roughly 15 feet wide and outward routes roughly twice that width. Carved stairs and built ramps sometimes carry alignments across cliffs. The Jackson Stairway above Chetro Ketl can be viewed from the Pueblo Alto Trail; it is closed to climbing.

The Great North Road runs from east of Pueblo Alto toward Kutz Canyon; the South Road leaves through South Gap toward the Red Mesa Valley. Many other known alignments are discontinuous. Researchers disagree about whether missing connections eroded away and about the relative importance of pilgrimage, symbolic connections, ordinary movement, and carrying goods. A diagram of the system should distinguish observed segments from reconstructed links.

pages.title: Hovenweep: springs, towers, and distinct communities
pages.intro: Hovenweep is a collection of separated ancestral places. Its canyon-head buildings connect architecture to springs, farming, and ceremonial life, while Goodman Point belongs to a different setting in the Montezuma Valley.

sections.heading: Six monument units, with Horseshoe and Hackberry distinguished

paragraphs.text: NPS counts six distinct monument units: Square Tower and Cajon in Utah; Holly, Cutthroat Castle, the combined Horseshoe/Hackberry boundary, and Goodman Point in Colorado. Horseshoe and Hackberry are also described as separate groups within their shared boundary. The table distinguishes those two places, producing seven named entries without implying seven separate administrative units.

The towers were made by ancestral Pueblo people. Their forms and placements vary, and their purposes should not be reduced to a single explanation. NPS presents ceremonial, calendrical, protective, storage, and residential possibilities; some descendant-community consultants emphasize rain prayer and relationships among springs, mountains, and water. These attributed interpretations should remain distinct from measured architecture.

rows.name: Square Tower Group
rows.dates: Most visible structures were built and used around 1200–1300 CE.
rows.architecture: Room blocks, towers, and complexes occupy the rims, boulders, slopes, and ledges of Little Ruin Canyon. NPS reports remains of nearly thirty kivas. The named Square Tower stands on a boulder near the canyon head.
rows.limits: Pueblo, Zuni, and Hopi descendants regard this as a continuing sacred place. Its name does not mean that cultural relationships ended when permanent residence shifted elsewhere.

rows.name: Cajon
rows.dates: Structures began in Pueblo I; greatest use about 900–1300 CE.
rows.architecture: A compact concentration of buildings at the southern edge of Cajon Mesa. Its towers and western building interact with seasonal sunlight and shadow in the interpretation presented by NPS.
rows.limits: Rain-prayer and timekeeping interpretations are attributed to tribal consultants, not established as the sole function of every building. The unit is reached through Navajo Nation land; use the designated public approach and parking.

rows.name: Holly
rows.dates: Primary use about 900–1300 CE.
rows.architecture: At the north fork of Keeley Canyon: five single-level masonry structures, three towers, possible kiva depressions, a dam, and a retaining wall. Holly Tower has two rooms and two stories on a large boulder.
rows.limits: The trail-visible petroglyph panel receives light beams around the summer solstice. NPS presents seasonal timekeeping and rain ceremony as interpretations informed by descendant consultants.

rows.name: Cutthroat Castle
rows.dates: Buildings were used across Pueblo I–III, about 750–1300 CE.
rows.architecture: Unlike the rim groups, its buildings lie within and along a drainage. The main three-story, D-shaped building sits on a boulder; nearby are towers, dwellings, and possible kiva depressions.
rows.limits: NPS identifies a probable above-ground kiva with an outer corridor. Neither its circular shape nor the modern name 'castle' proves a single exclusive function.

rows.name: Horseshoe
rows.dates: Evidence of occupation from around 450 CE; prominent stone construction belongs to the later ancestral Pueblo landscape, around and after 1200.
rows.architecture: Horseshoe House is a two-story, double-walled D-shaped building with four rooms around a circular room. A separate tower and room block occupy the point between drainage forks.
rows.limits: The central room is described as kiva-like. Horseshoe shares a protected boundary and trail with Hackberry; they should remain distinguishable as sites.

rows.name: Hackberry
rows.dates: Early use of the springs from around 450 CE; major masonry construction around 1200 and later.
rows.architecture: The largest complex in the monument retains traces of towers, rooms, terrace walls, and check dams near its spring, though comparatively little masonry stands upright.
rows.limits: Low surviving walls do not imply a minor settlement. It remains sacred to descendant communities.

rows.name: Goodman Point
rows.dates: Major thirteenth-century village; the cited NPS overview does not provide an exact construction sequence.
rows.architecture: A large, unexcavated pueblo in the Montezuma Valley, rather than a Cajon Mesa canyon-head tower group. NPS describes public architecture including great kivas, plazas, reservoirs, and enclosing walls in these village remains.
rows.limits: Buried architecture should not be reconstructed as fully known. Goodman Point is geographically and architecturally distinct from the five Cajon Mesa units.

paragraphs.text: Hovenweep's prominent canyon-head groups are associated with springs and seeps. A spring is a strong reason to locate buildings nearby, but proximity alone does not settle what each tower did. NPS explicitly leaves the purpose of Square Tower open and notes that its adjacent excavated kiva was not connected to it by a tunnel.

NPS asks visitors to remain on defined trails, avoid touching or entering structures, and leave artifacts in place. Outlying units require additional travel and walking; rough roads can become impassable when wet. Route conditions and permitted access should be checked with the monument before visiting.

pages.title: Mesa Verde: cliff villages within a much longer mesa-top history
pages.intro: The cliff dwellings are one part of Mesa Verde's settlement history. Mesa-top houses, farming communities, reservoirs, and ceremonial buildings reveal a landscape inhabited and repeatedly transformed over centuries.

paragraphs.text: NPS dates most cliff-dwelling construction to about 1180–1300 CE. Nearby seep springs helped make alcoves attractive as water supplies became less dependable. These were varied villages with living rooms, granaries, communal spaces, and kivas, fitted to particular rock faces and available space.

rows.name: Cliff Palace
rows.dates: About 1190–1280 CE.
rows.architecture: About 150 rooms and 23 kivas in a large alcove. Shaped sandstone, mortar, chinking stones, timber, and colored plaster formed its buildings.
rows.limits: Its exceptional size and abundant communal space suggest a wider community role; the English name does not identify a royal palace. Room counts are not resident counts.

rows.name: Balcony House
rows.dates: Late cliff-dwelling era; exact site sequence not supplied by this profile.
rows.architecture: 38 rooms and two kivas, with surviving balconies and two main plazas joined by a narrow passage.
rows.limits: The suggestion of two resident social groups is an archaeological interpretation, not an identified ethnic division.

rows.name: Long House
rows.dates: Late cliff-dwelling era.
rows.architecture: About 150 rooms, 21 kivas, a central gathering plaza, and carved water basins and drains along the rear of its Wetherill Mesa alcove.
rows.limits: A community-center role for neighboring villages is probable rather than directly documented.

rows.name: Spruce Tree House
rows.dates: Constructed about 1211–1278 CE.
rows.architecture: About 130 rooms and eight kivas in a natural alcove; the park's third-largest cliff dwelling.
rows.limits: NPS estimates 60–80 residents independently of room totals. View from designated overlooks; entry is closed because of unstable rock above the site.

rows.name: Step House
rows.dates: Two occupations: pithouses around 700 CE and masonry around 1200 CE.
rows.architecture: Early semi-subterranean houses and a later village of 27 rooms and three kivas share an alcove.
rows.limits: The two architectural episodes are separated by about five centuries, rather than constituting one continuously expanding village.

rows.name: Square Tower House
rows.dates: Late ancestral Pueblo cliff-dwelling landscape; exact dates not established by the cited visitor page.
rows.architecture: The park's tallest surviving structure, plus an intact kiva roof, original plaster and paint, and rock art.
rows.limits: The Mesa Top Loop overlook and restricted ranger-led visits offer different views. This site is separate from Hovenweep's Square Tower Group.

paragraphs.text: Far View shows that the move into alcoves was not universal. Some families continued living on the mesa top while nearby cliff villages were occupied. Fields, houses, water storage, and paths connected these places; a simple progression from mesa-top settlement to complete cliff occupation obscures that coexistence.

rows.name: Far View Community
rows.dates: About 800–1300 CE in the cited place profile.
rows.architecture: Far View House, Pipe Shrine House, Coyote Village, Megalithic House, Far View Tower, and a now-dry reservoir form the visitor circuit through a larger farming landscape.
rows.limits: The six displayed places are a sample of a much wider community. NPS suggests at least 35 occupied villages within half a square mile in the mid-1100s.

rows.name: Badger House Community
rows.dates: A sequence spanning roughly 600 years, including an early pithouse around 650 CE.
rows.architecture: Four interpretive sites: Modified Basketmaker Pithouse, Developmental Pueblo village, Badger House, and Two Raven House, on Wetherill Mesa.
rows.limits: These are sites from a long sequence, not four necessarily contemporary neighborhoods.

rows.name: Cedar Tree Tower and nearby farming terraces
rows.dates: Tower-kiva complexes were chiefly built about 1100–1300 CE.
rows.architecture: A mesa-top tower associated with a kiva. Nearby check dams slowed runoff, trapped soil, and retained moisture for crops.
rows.limits: Tower use is unresolved: ceremonial and communication functions are proposals. The agricultural interpretation of check dams rests on their form and hydrological effect.

rows.name: Sun Temple
rows.dates: Mesa-top construction continued into the 1200s; precise dating is difficult without roof timbers or a substantial domestic assemblage.
rows.architecture: An intentionally D-shaped complex with thick masonry walls, 24 excavated rooms, three circular structures within the main complex, and another detached circular structure.
rows.limits: NPS describes a likely communal or ceremonial building. Whether it was left unfinished or intentionally unroofed, and the details of possible astronomical use, remain open questions.

pages.title: Canyons of the Ancients: Lowry, Sand Canyon, and Castle Rock
pages.intro: These public sites represent different moments and forms of ancestral Pueblo settlement in southwestern Colorado. Lowry's longer growth contrasts with the concentrated thirteenth-century histories of Sand Canyon Pueblo and Castle Rock Pueblo.

paragraphs.text: Canyons of the Ancients protects a broad cultural landscape northwest of Mesa Verde and Cortez. Its thousands of recorded places belong to histories extending well beyond the three pueblos shown here. The visitor center and museum provides context before a visit; in the Sand Canyon/Rock Creek management area, travel is restricted to designated routes.

rows.name: Lowry Pueblo
rows.dates: Built over an earlier community around 1060 CE and inhabited for about 165 years. Major additions occurred about 1085–1170.
rows.architecture: Grew from a small settlement to about 40 rooms, eight kivas, and a great kiva. Additions included Kiva B, known for painted decoration.
rows.limits: The final architectural inventory accumulated over time. Forty rooms does not mean forty residents, and Chaco-related architecture alone does not establish direct political control from Chaco.

rows.name: Sand Canyon Pueblo
rows.dates: Construction began in the late 1240s or early 1250s and continued into the late 1270s.
rows.architecture: An estimated 420 rooms, 90 kivas, fourteen towers, a plaza, a great kiva, and a D-shaped bi-wall building. A substantial masonry wall enclosed much of the village around a canyon-head setting.
rows.limits: Counts are estimates for a complex archaeological site. Excavated structures and archived study units are not the same as all structures in the pueblo. A wall had defensive potential, but its presence does not explain every aspect of community life.

rows.name: Castle Rock Pueblo
rows.dates: Occupied from the 1260s into the 1280s; occupation ended abruptly around the mid-1280s.
rows.architecture: A village constructed at the base and on top of a prominent sandstone butte. Crow Canyon interprets the position as probably selected in part for defensibility.
rows.limits: Excavation evidence indicates a violent ending. That event should not be expanded into an unsupported identity for the attackers or a single explanation for all regional migration. Crow Canyon estimates 75–150 residents; this is an estimate, not a census.

sections.heading: What excavation can and cannot establish

paragraphs.text: Sand Canyon's excavated rooms, kivas, refuse, and tree-ring samples support a reconstruction of a lived-in village that grew through additions and collective building projects. Some reused or older timbers predate the main construction sequence; individual early wood dates should not automatically be treated as the date the village was founded.

Castle Rock's abrupt violent ending is a site-specific finding. Lowry's different chronology and Sand Canyon's much larger architectural footprint caution against treating all places in the monument as one synchronous settlement or one uniform community. Dates, room totals, and excavation coverage need to remain attached to the individual site.

pages.title: Inca civilization: the Tawantinsuyu and its connected landscapes
pages.intro: The Inca state linked communities, production zones, sacred places, and administrative centres across the Andes. Its roads and monumental architecture drew on earlier Andean histories and the work of many communities. Machu Picchu is one estate within this wider history.

paragraphs.text: Cusco was the imperial capital, with religious, governmental, and royal spaces forming a planned urban ensemble. The fifteenth-century Inca remodeling continued a much longer local settlement history. Surviving streets and walls now form part of a living city shaped again during colonial and later periods.

Imperial chronology remains a research question rather than a reliable date stamp for every site. Ogburn's 2012 analysis questions how colonial writers converted accounts of conquest into a linear sequence and argues for independent radiocarbon frameworks. Regional expansion, a ruler's life, construction, and a sample's age are different events.

Diversity within the state is visible at a small scale in Machu Picchu's burial sample. The 2023 genomic study supports a varied attendant community rather than a population drawn solely from the immediate Cusco region. Its authors combine ancestry results with archaeology and history; their sampled individuals should not stand for every imperial population.

sections.heading: Roads and the institutions along them

paragraphs.text: UNESCO describes four main routes originating at Cusco and linking with smaller roads. The wider network incorporated pre-Inca infrastructure and supported communication, movement, supplies, and state administration. Bridges, steps, paving, and drainage adapted to different terrains. The World Heritage property selects representative sections and associated places; it is not the full surviving network.

Peru's road-registration guide identifies a major highland longitudinal axis between Quito and Mendoza through Cusco. Huánuco Pampa's official inventory places that administrative centre on the Cusco–Quito corridor. The diagram below reduces this long system to four named reference places and three corridor connections; many intermediate settlements and branches are omitted.

rows.name: Road engineering
rows.dates: Built and adapted over centuries; major imperial expansion in the fifteenth century.
rows.architecture: Variable surfaces, retaining walls, stairs, bridges, and drains negotiated sharply different environments.
rows.limits: Do not assign one construction date or identical design to the whole network.

rows.name: Longitudinal and connecting roads
rows.dates: Inca-period organization incorporates earlier routes.
rows.architecture: The highland spine was complemented by coastal routes, transverse connections, and links between drainage basins.
rows.limits: The small diagram shows a selected corridor, not all four imperial quarters or a complete road inventory.

rows.name: Huánuco Pampa: administration and storage
rows.dates: Inca administrative centre; no precise foundation year established here.
rows.architecture: A planned highland centre on the Cusco–Quito road, with large storage facilities. Colcas included circular and rectangular buildings.
rows.limits: Storehouse totals are archaeological inventories, not counts of resident households.

rows.name: A living cultural network
rows.dates: Ancient routes with continuing community relationships.
rows.architecture: Selected road sections remain associated with local knowledge, maintenance practices, exchange, and cultural traditions.
rows.limits: The end of the Inca state did not end Andean peoples or all uses of its roads.

paragraphs.text: State ceremony linked the ruler and Inti, the Sun, with offerings and sacred places. Smithsonian interpretation also emphasizes Pachamama and roads as connections with a spiritual universe. Imperial worship and local sacred relationships should not be flattened into one identical practice everywhere. Inca-period religion is reconstructed through material remains, historical testimony, and living Andean traditions, each with a different relationship to the past.

sections.heading: Languages: Quechua and a debated court language

paragraphs.text: Quechua was important in the Inca world, but the empire incorporated speakers of many languages. Aymara and Puquina also belong to debates over its linguistic history. Cerrón-Palomino proposes Puquina connections for sparse names and reports of a special court language; this is a historical-linguistic hypothesis, not a demonstrated language for every ruler or resident. Language affiliation, political allegiance, and biological ancestry are separate questions.

A kingdom centred on Cusco expanded into Tawantinsuyu through military campaigns and state integration, especially during the fifteenth century. Conventional royal dates are being revised against radiocarbon evidence. Spanish invasion, Indigenous alliances, and the capture of Atahualpa in 1532 disrupted imperial rule; conquest and colonial transformation were processes rather than the disappearance of Andean peoples. Languages, communities, and traditions continued beyond the empire.

pages.title: Machu Picchu and the Inca heartland: architecture, water, and changing chronologies
pages.intro: Machu Picchu is a planned mountain settlement within a larger landscape of roads, terraces, sacred places, and royal estates. Its architecture and engineering can be described more securely than an exact construction year for every building.

sections.heading: A ridge settlement within a larger landscape

paragraphs.text: The archaeological settlement stands on a steep ridge about 2,430 metres above sea level, within the much larger mixed cultural and natural World Heritage sanctuary. UNESCO describes roughly 200 structures, organized into upper and lower parts and agricultural and residential areas. That approximate structural inventory is neither a count of houses nor an estimate of permanent residents.

The royal-estate interpretation connects the site with Pachacuti and an attendant community. A 2023 study generated genome-wide data for 34 people buried at Machu Picchu and compared them with 34 individuals from the Cusco area. The authors found considerable ancestry diversity extending across the empire and Amazonia. These sampled burials are not a census, and genetic affinities do not identify a person's language, named ethnic group, or precise place of birth.

rows.name: Main settlement and central open spaces
rows.dates: Fifteenth-century construction in the UNESCO overview; occupation chronology is discussed separately below.
rows.architecture: Stone-built compounds, open spaces, ramps, stairs, and terraces fit a narrow ridge. Upper and lower areas and agricultural and residential zones form an integrated plan.
rows.limits: The World Heritage property includes surrounding mountains and ecosystems; its boundary is much larger than the built settlement. Broad functional labels do not establish the exact use of every room.

rows.name: Temple of the Sun
rows.dates: Inca-period monument; no independently verified room-specific construction year in the cited description.
rows.architecture: A curved masonry building fitted over a large natural granite outcrop, with trapezoidal windows and a finely worked doorway.
rows.limits: Architectural integration with bedrock is observable. The modern building name and proposed astronomical roles require interpretation.

rows.name: Temple of the Three Windows
rows.dates: Inca-period construction; exact building dates remain unspecified here.
rows.architecture: A rectangular building beside a principal ceremonial open space, distinguished by three openings and finely fitted large stone blocks.
rows.limits: Describe the windows and masonry separately from claims about their symbolic meaning. A name does not establish a complete original ritual programme.

rows.name: Intiwatana hill and carved rock
rows.dates: Inca-period reshaping of the hill; exact carving date is not established by the cited study.
rows.architecture: A worked bedrock feature crowns a terraced eminence associated with nearby ceremonial open spaces and buildings. The hill, terraces, paths, and outcrop form one designed ensemble.
rows.limits: Astronomical interpretations should distinguish measured alignments from a fully demonstrated calendar or single exclusive function. 'Intiwatana' is also used for other places; this row concerns the hill within the llaqta.

sections.heading: Terraces, drinking water, and drainage worked together

paragraphs.text: Water supply and storm drainage solved different problems. Field research documented spring collection and gravity delivery to fountains, while engineering analysis examined how heavy rainfall moved through and away from the steep built site. A fountain's capacity should not be converted into an observed resident population, and a successful drainage design does not mean that every wall or slope was immune to movement.

rows.name: Agricultural terraces
rows.dates: Inca construction; the selected engineering study does not assign one building year to all terraces.
rows.architecture: Retaining walls contain planting soil above progressively coarser, permeable fills. The terraces support cultivation while controlling runoff and erosion.
rows.limits: The published field investigation found no branches from the main supply canal irrigating the upper agricultural terraces. Do not assume every terrace was irrigated simply because water channels exist nearby.

rows.name: Spring, supply canal, and fountains
rows.dates: Inca water system documented by fieldwork begun under a 1994 archaeological permit.
rows.architecture: A spring on the north slope of Machu Picchu mountain fed a gravity canal measured at 749 metres, supplying sixteen fountains in the settlement.
rows.limits: Measured spring yields varied seasonally. The engineering paper's proposed occupation dates and population figures are older interpretations; neither hydraulic capacity nor those dates overrides newer archaeological dating.

rows.name: Surface and subsurface drainage
rows.dates: Inca infrastructure; analyzed in a 1999 engineering study.
rows.architecture: An extensive drainage system addressed steep slopes and rainfall approaching two metres annually. It forms essential infrastructure beneath and between the visible buildings and terraces.
rows.limits: Rainfall values describe an engineering context, not a fixed annual climate for every year of occupation. Drainage performance and later conservation condition are separate questions.

paragraphs.text: A traditional historical model links Pachacuti's accession to 1438 and places Machu Picchu's beginnings around 1450–1460. That model depends heavily on colonial accounts. Ogburn's 2012 study challenged the wider imperial sequence using dates from Chamical in Ecuador and argued that conquest narratives may combine geographic and chronological order. Its results concern imperial expansion; they do not directly date Machu Picchu's individual buildings.

Burger and colleagues' 2021 AMS study dated bone and teeth from burials in four cemetery areas and inferred occupation around 1420–1532. A separate Bayesian study of Machu Picchu, Chachabamba, and Choqesuysuy modeled a small set of archaeological samples. Its Machu Picchu first-event estimate was 1422–1448 at 68.2% probability in one model, widening to 1421–1476 when allowing for wood's inbuilt age. These are different datasets and model outputs, not interchangeable exact foundation years. Calibration assumptions, residual charcoal, and the event actually sampled matter.

Cusco, Ollantaytambo, Pisaq, and Choquequirao provide different comparisons: an imperial capital reshaped by later occupation, a planned valley town, dispersed estate architecture, and a mountain complex with extensive terraces. Similar masonry or landscape design does not make them simultaneous foundations or establish identical purposes. Each site's building history needs its own archaeological evidence.

rows.name: Cusco: imperial centre and later city
rows.dates: Major Inca remodeling in the fifteenth century over a much older settlement; colonial construction followed the sixteenth-century conquest.
rows.architecture: Religious and administrative buildings, royal compounds, finely cut walls, streets, and canchas survive within a continuously occupied city. Qoricancha is a key surviving component of the Inca ensemble.
rows.limits: The capital's long occupation cannot be assigned the short chronology of the empire. Later buildings often incorporate or overlie earlier fabric; an Inca wall and the building above it may have different dates.

rows.name: Ollantaytambo
rows.dates: Imperial and late Inca phases; chroniclers differ about its royal builder.
rows.architecture: A planned settlement beside the Patakancha near its Urubamba confluence. Qosqo Ayllu and Araccama Ayllu include plazas, palaces, enclosures, and shrines, complemented by terraces, storehouses, and walls.
rows.limits: The culture authority reports Sarmiento's attribution to Pachacuti and Garcilaso's to Wiracocha. These are historical attributions, not a resolved construction date for the entire complex.

rows.name: Pisaq / Pisac
rows.dates: Inca estate traditionally associated with Pachacuti; no precise foundation year established here.
rows.architecture: Dispersed terraces, agricultural platforms, domestic compounds, and ceremonial buildings occupy ridges above the Sacred Valley, near the approach from Cusco and routes toward Paucartambo.
rows.limits: The royal-estate interpretation is explicitly linked by the culture authority to Sarmiento de Gamboa. Its extent and varied sectors should not be collapsed into a single temple or fortress.

rows.name: Choquequirao
rows.dates: Inca complex; colonial-source interpretations associate an estate with Tupac Inca Yupanqui or Pachacuti rather than securely dating every sector.
rows.architecture: A mountain settlement above the right bank of the Apurimac, with plazas, terraces, and built compounds. Western terraces include pale-stone figurative designs, notably camelids, set into terrace walls.
rows.limits: It is a separate place from Machu Picchu. Differing official inventories count terrace motifs differently, so no combined figure total is asserted here; symbolic interpretations also remain proposals.

pages.title: Maya centres: different cities, histories, and monumental plans
pages.intro: These four public archaeological centres belong to a much larger Maya world. Their temples, palaces, inscriptions, reservoirs, and open spaces record distinct dynasties and changing regional relationships, rather than one capital governing an unchanging empire.

paragraphs.text: A site's broad occupation span is not the date of every surviving monument. Buildings could cover earlier structures, and carved texts could commemorate events long before their own dedication. Compare the material sequence, named rulers, and dated inscriptions at each centre before assigning a single founding or ending year to the whole Maya world.

rows.name: Tikal, Guatemala
rows.dates: Occupation extends from the Preclassic into the early tenth century; the principal monumental ensembles accumulated across many episodes.
rows.architecture: The Great Plaza, Lost World complex, twin-pyramid groups, palaces, ball courts, causeways, and reservoirs form parts of a much wider settlement.
rows.limits: The park boundary, monumental core, and residential landscape have different extents. Reservoirs and peripheral settlements are essential context; visible pyramids are only part of the city.

rows.name: Palenque, Chiapas, Mexico
rows.dates: A major Classic-period capital, especially prominent during the sixth through eighth centuries.
rows.architecture: The Palace, Temple of the Inscriptions, and Cross Group combine masonry buildings, modeled decoration, and extensive dynastic and mythological texts. Pakal's seventh-century reign is central to its monumental history.
rows.limits: A ruler's reign does not date every wall. Tombs, temple superstructures, texts, and later additions need separate archaeological histories.

rows.name: Copán, Honduras
rows.dates: A Classic dynasty began in the fifth century; the centre's political and monumental history changed substantially before early tenth-century abandonment.
rows.architecture: The Acropolis, plazas, sculpted stelae, and Hieroglyphic Stairway connect public space, royal monuments, and written accounts of dynastic authority.
rows.limits: The inscribed stairway is a historical monument as well as architecture. Interpretations must consider displaced blocks and reconstruction, rather than assuming the visible stair text survives entirely in original order.

rows.name: Chichén Itzá, Yucatán, Mexico
rows.dates: Monumental building spans different phases, including important northern ensembles around the Terminal Classic and Early Postclassic transition.
rows.architecture: El Castillo, the Temple of the Warriors, columned spaces, the Great Ball Court, and El Caracol occupy a landscape with cenotes and earlier building groups.
rows.limits: Architectural connections with central Mexico do not by themselves prove a single invasion date or the ethnicity of every builder. Later written traditions and archaeological construction sequences should remain distinguishable.

pages.title: Maya cultures: writing, ritual, and continuing communities
pages.intro: Maya history includes many languages, regional traditions, and political centres. Ancient monumental cities and contemporary Maya communities are connected histories, while particular practices and institutions changed over time.

paragraphs.text: Ceremony linked calendars, farming, sacred places, and political authority, with substantial local variation. Smithsonian accounts describe living Yucatec offerings connected with rain and harvests and highland Guatemalan ceremonies marking sacred-calendar cycles. These contemporary practices illuminate continuing relationships with time and land; they should not be projected unchanged onto every ancient temple or dynasty. Archaeological images and inscriptions add different kinds of evidence.

Maya is not the name of one uniform spoken language. Smithsonian describes more than thirty living Mayan languages. Ancient writing combined signs for whole words with syllabic signs; decipherment relates signs to the languages encoded in particular texts. A carved inscription can preserve royal names, events, and calendrical statements, but script affiliation does not establish the everyday speech of every resident of a city.

Maya centres developed through long Preclassic and Classic histories. During the late first millennium, many southern lowland dynasties and cities lost population or political power, while other regions followed different trajectories. Archaeologist Jeremy Sabloff emphasizes political fragmentation and population movement rather than the disappearance of Maya people. Northern centres and highland communities continued, followed by profound colonial disruptions and continuing Maya histories into the present.

pages.title: Cahokia: earthworks and open spaces of a major Mississippian centre
pages.intro: Cahokia stands in the American Bottom near present-day Collinsville, Illinois. Its monumental core belonged to a wider agricultural and settlement landscape. Earthwork dimensions and mound totals are architectural evidence, not direct resident counts.

sections.heading: Reading three parts of the centre

paragraphs.text: UNESCO places Cahokia's greatest prominence around 1050–1150 CE within a longer Mississippian history. Mounds served different purposes: some supported buildings, others contained burials or marked important places. The present protected property, surviving mounds, and the original metropolitan landscape are different inventories. Modern reconstruction, erosion, and excavation also affect what a visitor sees today.

rows.name: Monks Mound and the Grand Plaza
rows.dates: Built and enlarged during Cahokia's Mississippian occupation; not a single construction event.
rows.architecture: A large, multiterraced earthen platform dominates the central open-space ensemble. Its summit supported a substantial building, while the plaza created space for gathering and public activity.
rows.limits: Reconstructing leadership roles requires interpretation of architecture and associated evidence. The modern name refers to much later monks and is not the original Indigenous name.

rows.name: Woodhenge
rows.dates: Mississippian-period post-circle constructions, known through excavated post settings; the standing display is reconstructed.
rows.architecture: Timber circles west of the monumental centre are interpreted in relation to seasonal solar observations. The reconstructed posts help explain a vanished wooden structure.
rows.limits: The modern timber is not original surviving wood. A seasonal alignment supports observation and timekeeping interpretations, but does not independently recover every associated ritual.

rows.name: Mound 72
rows.dates: A sequence of mortuary deposits and mound-building episodes within Cahokia's earlier monumental history.
rows.architecture: A comparatively small ridge-topped mound covered complex burial deposits and associated objects, providing evidence of mortuary ceremony and social distinctions.
rows.limits: Later reanalysis revised influential interpretations of the beaded burial. Avoid repeating the older male-warrior-and-retainers narrative as settled fact; biological assessments and social identities are distinct questions.

pages.title: Mississippian cultures: connected societies, not one nation
pages.intro: Mississippian is an archaeological label for diverse communities sharing aspects of agriculture, settlement, material culture, and ceremony across much of the eastern and southeastern United States. Cahokia was an important centre within this varied world.

paragraphs.text: Mounds, public gathering places, mortuary deposits, and images on shell, copper, ceramics, and stone provide evidence of ceremonial life. Illinois State Museum stresses that religious ideas are reconstructed by combining archaeology with historical accounts, not read directly from objects. Shared symbols across regions suggest connections, while local differences and changing practices caution against assuming one uniform religion or an identical role for every mound.

The archaeological category does not identify a single language or tribe. At Cahokia, researchers infer a population drawn from different regions, likely speaking multiple languages or dialects. No securely deciphered local writing provides a citywide linguistic census. Connections with later Indigenous nations are essential historical evidence, but should not be converted into a simple one-to-one language assignment for every earlier town or ceremonial centre.

sections.heading: Rise, changing centres, and continuing communities

paragraphs.text: Maize farming, exchange, migration, and new forms of political organization contributed to the growth of mound-centred communities, with different regional chronologies. At Ocmulgee, the Macon Plateau centre diminished by about 1200 while other Mississippian places continued; Lamar developed later nearby. Warfare, population movement, and colonial violence and disease reshaped communities at different times. The decline of a centre is not the disappearance of its descendants.

pages.title: Pacific monumental places: four distinct island histories
pages.intro: This collection compares monuments across a vast ocean without treating them as one culture. Pohnpei, Tonga, Rapa Nui, and Hawaiʻi have distinct languages, political histories, ceremonial traditions, and relationships with their ancestral places.

paragraphs.text: Nan Madol combined chiefly residences, ceremonial places, and mortuary structures within Pohnpei's political history. UNESCO relates it to the Saudeleur era and continuing Nahnmwarki institutions, rather than a vanished people. Pohnpeian is a living language associated with the island; this contemporary linguistic connection is not a decoded record of every ancient resident's speech. Architecture and oral traditions provide complementary kinds of historical evidence.

rows.name: Nan Madol, Pohnpei
rows.dates: UNESCO broadly dates the surviving stone palaces, temples, tombs, and residential domains to about 1200–1500 CE.
rows.architecture: More than one hundred constructed islets, basalt walls, coral fill, and waterways form a monumental complex off southeastern Pohnpei.
rows.limits: Islet counts are not house or population totals. Separate individual construction dates from the broad Saudeleur-era range; customary ownership and spiritual significance continue.

sections.heading: Tonga: capitals, tombs, and continuing chiefly histories

paragraphs.text: Heketā and Lapaha belong to the history of Tuʻi Tonga authority. Tonga's national submission associates royal tombs and ongoing burial traditions with both spiritual and political power. Tongan is a distinct living language; neither its relationship to other Polynesian languages nor similar stonework makes these monuments part of a single Pacific state. Genealogical traditions, recorded histories, and archaeological dates should be identified separately.

rows.name: Heketā and Lapaha, Tongatapu
rows.dates: The trilithon is traditionally attributed to Tuʻitātui around 1200; royal tomb development at Lapaha has a longer, varied history.
rows.architecture: Haʻamonga ʻa Maui uses two upright coral-limestone slabs and a lintel. Lapaha's langi are stepped earthen funerary platforms faced with stone.
rows.limits: These places are on Tonga's UNESCO Tentative List. The submission explicitly questions the origins of later sundial claims; oral attributions are not precise laboratory dates.

sections.heading: Rapa Nui: ancestors, platforms, and later ceremonial changes

paragraphs.text: Moai represented ancestors within Rapa Nui's own ceremonial landscape. Ahu platforms, quarries, rock art, houses, and the later Orongo ceremonial village record varied activities and changing practices. Rapa Nui is also a living Polynesian language supported by contemporary revitalization programmes. Political and ritual transformation and the severe effects of colonial intrusion should remain distinct from unsupported claims that monument building ended in one simple ecological collapse.

rows.name: Rapa Nui: Rano Raraku, ahu, and Orongo
rows.dates: Monumental and ceremonial traditions changed over centuries; the UNESCO synthesis places major works broadly within the eleventh–seventeenth centuries.
rows.architecture: Rano Raraku preserves carving stages; ahu carried ancestral statues, including the fifteen-moai ensemble at Ahu Tongariki. Orongo has a different ceremonial and architectural character.
rows.limits: The broad span is not a secure first-settlement date. Standing displays and re-erected statues require separate conservation histories; no island-wide resident count is inferred.

sections.heading: Hawaiʻi: a historically dated temple and political unification

paragraphs.text: Puʻukoholā links a particular Hawaiian heiau with Kamehameha's rise, prophecy, and worship associated with Kū. NPS places it within a hierarchical chiefly society and the kapu system, which was overturned in 1819. ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi is the Indigenous Hawaiian language and remains central to cultural continuity. These events have their own historical chronology, distinct from the earlier monuments of Pohnpei, Tonga, or Rapa Nui.

rows.name: Puʻukoholā Heiau, Kawaihae, Hawaiʻi Island
rows.dates: Built under Kamehameha in 1790–1791, a specifically documented late-eighteenth-century project.
rows.architecture: A substantial dry-stone temple platform occupies a coastal hill. Its construction and dedication formed part of Kamehameha's struggle for power.
rows.limits: The heiau's completion is distinct from the later unification of the Hawaiian Islands. It is a continuing culturally significant place, not a generic example of all Polynesian religion.
